samples.text: As of this evening, the holding position rests on a manual fix. The working basis is manual agency code mapping override applied to complete valuation for the period. That override is justified because the defect is now confirmed: stale legacy-to-new agency code mapping in the reference data register. Correcting the mapping by hand for the affected codes lets the period proceed without waiting for a structural repair to the register, which cannot be designed and tested inside the incident window. The arrangement is provisional. It covers this period only, it depends on the engineers who applied it, and it has not yet had the review that a change to reference data would normally receive. Anyone deciding whether to wait can plan on the valuation being available on this basis. What they cannot assume is that the underlying mapping is fixed. Until the register is corrected and owned, the next period carries the same risk, and this holding arrangement would have to be repeated.

The established cause is stale legacy-to-new agency code mapping in the reference data register. The inventory valuation service resolves agency codes through that mapping, and entries that no longer matched their cloud counterparts left the run unable to value the affected records. This was not the first explanation on the table, because the incident was initially attributed to overnight ERP outage. That theory fitted the timing of an overnight batch and was the obvious suspect. It was closed on evidence rather than opinion: ERP logs show no interruption during the valuation window. With the upstream system cleared, the investigation turned to the reference data that feeds the run and found the stale entries there. The deeper finding sits with the product hierarchy sync service, where the root cause classification reads control failure: the mapping table has no registered owner and no required reviewer.
